primer.text: Biodiversity measures the variety of life, from species richness to the variation inside each species. This note defines the term, shows what high biodiversity looks like, explains why species interdependence makes diverse ecosystems stable, and names the human activities that erode it.

lessons.title: Counting Life's Variety
lessons.opening: Biodiversity means the range and variety among the different species of organisms on Earth or inside one ecosystem, and it weighs not just how many species live there but the variation inside each species, where they live and how many of them there are.
keyPoints: Biodiversity covers the range and variety among the different species of organisms on Earth or inside one ecosystem.
It considers species richness, the variation within each species, distribution and population size.
High biodiversity describes an environment with many different species showing much variation, evenly distributed.
Human activities such as waste production, deforestation and global warming reduce biodiversity.

low.restatement: Count the species, weigh the differences inside each, and check they spread across the area.
low.analogy: A fruit basket judged on how many fruit types it holds, how varied each type is, and how evenly they fill the basket.
low.examPointer: The definition has two scopes — on Earth, or within one ecosystem — quote both if asked to define.

medium.restatement: The term is deliberately broad: species richness is only one strand, and the variation within each species, its distribution across the study area and its population size all feed the judgement; human pressures such as waste, deforestation and warming erode every strand at once.
medium.analogy: Judging a choir not by headcount alone but by range of voices, spread across the stage and balance of sections.
medium.examPointer: For high biodiversity, quote the full recipe: many species, much variation, even distribution.

options.text: The range and variety among the different species of organisms on Earth or inside one ecosystem
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The number of animals in one zoo
options.explanation: One collection does not define biodiversity.

options.text: The weight of all living matter
options.explanation: Biomass measures mass; biodiversity counts variety.

options.text: Only the rarest species on Earth
options.explanation: Rarity is a piece, not the whole definition.

options.text: Species richness, variation within species, distribution and population size
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Only the total count of species
options.explanation: The definition weighs more than richness alone.
No laboratory restriction applies.
All species count, large or small.

check.stem: A meadow holds many species, evenly spread, each showing wide variation. How is its biodiversity described?

options.text: High, because richness, variation and even distribution all score well
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The named features all point the other way.
Commonness does not set biodiversity.
Variation adds to biodiversity, it never cancels it.

options.text: Waste production, deforestation and global warming
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Protection schemes aim to preserve biodiversity.
Rotation is a managed practice, not the named reducers.
Recycling reduces waste pressure rather than raising it.

check.stem: Why does a forest with one tree species score lower than a mixed woodland?

options.text: Because fewer species means lower species richness and less variation
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Height is not part of biodiversity.

options.text: Because one species always dies out
options.explanation: The scoring rests on richness and variation, not certain loss.
Mixed woodlands show they can.

check.modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the range and variety among the different species of organisms on Earth, or inside one ecosystem.

check.stem: State two features biodiversity considers beyond species richness.
check.modelAnswer: Biodiversity also considers the variation inside each species, its distribution and its population size.

check.stem: Explain why even distribution raises the biodiversity score of a habitat.
check.modelAnswer: Even distribution raises the score because species spread across the study area show a healthier, less clumped pattern, which is part of how biodiversity is judged.

check.stem: A landfill leaks waste beside a species-rich marsh. Predict the biodiversity trend.
check.modelAnswer: Biodiversity falls as waste pollution damages the marsh, cutting species richness and shifting populations below their healthy levels.

lessons.title: Why Variety Keeps Ecosystems Steady
lessons.opening: Species lean on each other for food, shelter and a stable physical environment, so a habitat with high biodiversity weathers shocks better, since no single population depends on just one partner for survival.
keyPoints: Species rely on one another for food, shelter and maintenance of the physical environment.
High biodiversity lowers how much one species depends on another, steadying ecosystems.
Populations with high diversity are more resilient to sudden environmental impacts or disease.
In a rich food web, the loss of one prey species rarely wipes out its predators, which switch to alternatives.

low.restatement: More species means more backup options, so losing one partner hurts less.
low.analogy: A diversified investment portfolio: one crashed share cannot bankrupt the holder.
low.examPointer: Use the food web case: foxes and hawks survive losing mice because rabbits, frogs and sparrows remain.

medium.restatement: Interdependence runs through food chains, nesting shelter and physical services like roots binding soil; when biodiversity is high these dependencies multiply, so shocks and diseases spread through fewer essential links and populations can switch partners instead of collapsing.
medium.analogy: A power grid with many generators: one station failing dims the lights but cannot black out the city.
medium.examPointer: Tie resilience to reduced dependence — that phrase is the marking point for stability questions.

check.stem: Give the three supports species draw from each other.

options.text: Food, shelter and maintenance of the physical environment
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The named supports are food, shelter and environment upkeep.
None of these are the stated supports.
Scent may aid feeding, but the stated triple differs.

check.stem: How do tree roots support other species?

options.text: They steady the soil, which keeps a stable habitat for other plants
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Soil stability is the named role.
Global cooling is not the stated mechanism.
Roots support habitat stability, not direct feeding.

check.stem: Why is high biodiversity safer for a food web?

options.text: Because predators hold several prey options, so one loss does not starve them
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Webs still change; biodiversity cushions the blows.
Roles stay mixed; the safety comes from options.
The point is alternative prey, not a diet switch to plants.

check.stem: In a food web where mice are wiped out, what happens to the predators such as foxes and hawks?

options.text: Their numbers might decrease, but alternatives like rabbits and frogs keep them alive
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Mice are not their only food source, so they persist.
Losing a food source presses numbers down, not up.
Migration out is not the stated outcome.

check.stem: Why do diverse populations resist disease better?

options.text: Because high diversity makes populations more resilient to sudden impacts or disease
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because diseases cannot exist in diverse places
options.explanation: Diseases exist everywhere; resilience is the point.

options.text: Because diverse individuals never infect others
options.explanation: Infection still happens; recovery and persistence improve.
Medicine is not the mechanism named.

check.stem: State three things species depend on each other for.
check.modelAnswer: Species rely on one another for food, shelter and maintenance of the physical environment.

check.stem: State the effect of high biodiversity on ecosystem stability.
check.modelAnswer: High biodiversity steadies ecosystems by lowering how much one species depends on another.

check.stem: Explain why losing one prey species seldom wipes out its predator in a diverse web.
check.modelAnswer: In a diverse web the predator holds alternative prey, so losing one species presses its numbers down without starving it entirely.

check.stem: A woodland loses its mice to disease but holds rabbits, frogs and sparrows. Judge the outcome.
check.modelAnswer: Foxes and hawks decrease but survive, since the remaining biodiversity supplies alternative prey, showing the ecosystem holds sufficient variety to absorb the shock.

glossary.definition: The range and variety among the different species of organisms on Earth or inside one ecosystem.
The number of different species present in an area.
The mutual reliance of species on each other for food, shelter and a stable environment.
